findings.title: No library-coordination guard: a Connection* minted by the duckdb wheel is passed to a possibly-different libduckdb resolved by numbduck's JIT bindings (cross-library type confusion)
findings.category: type-confusion / trusting external memory layout across two library instances
findings.description: extract_connection_ptr recovers the raw Connection* out of the duckdb Python wheel's C++ DuckDBPyConnection object (id(conn)+16 then +32, lines 59/62) and then hands that pointer straight to ducklib.duckdb_query / ducklib.duckdb_destroy_result (lines 67-68). Those two symbols are NOT resolved from the wheel — they are resolved by numba/LLVM's JIT linker against whatever libduckdb numbduck's loader put into the global symbol namespace via RTLD_GLOBAL (numbduck/utils.py load_duckdb -> load_lib_path). On Linux these coincide (numbduck loads the wheel's own _duckdb.so, so the Connection* and duckdb_query come from the same binary). On macOS, and on any host where the wheel strips the C API, load_duckdb takes a fallback path (loader.md 5a/5b): it loads a *standalone* libduckdb from NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB, from a Homebrew/usr-local path (_MACOS_LIBDUCKDB_SEARCH_PATHS), or a downloaded universal dylib. A brew or env-pointed libduckdb can be a DIFFERENT VERSION/BUILD than the wheel's statically-linked duckdb (brew's copy is whatever brew installed, unrelated to duckdb.__version__). Passing a Connection* created by build A into build B's C-API entry points is undefined behavior: the internal Connection/ClientContext object layout that duckdb_query dereferences is not an ABI-stable contract across builds. The sibling bridge this file is explicitly modeled on refuses exactly this: numbox pysqlite_bridge.libraries_coordinated() (pysqlite_bridge.py:93-107) compares the bindings' linked version against the Python module's linked version and extract_connection_ptr RAISES (pysqlite_bridge.py:159-167) rather than cross a pointer between two mismatched libraries. pybridge.py has no analogous gate; there is no comparison of duckdb.__version__ (the wheel) against duckdb_library_version() (the JIT-linked lib) anywhere before the pointer is used.
findings.impact: On the macOS/standalone fallback path, or whenever NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB / a brew libduckdb points at a duckdb whose build differs from the wheel, duckdb_query dereferences a Connection* laid out by a different duckdb build. The SELECT 1 'validation' cannot catch this (a wrong-layout deref is UB, not a returnable rc) so it manifests as an interpreter segfault or silent memory corruption at the first C-API call, not a clean error. Same failure class numbox deliberately guards against.
findings.recommendation: Before trusting/returning the pointer, add a coordination check mirroring numbox: compare duckdb.__version__ (the wheel whose object you are walking) against the loaded library's duckdb_library_version() (the lib whose C API you call) and raise RuntimeError with remediation guidance (set NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB to the wheel's own lib) when they disagree. At minimum call it out in the docstring that this bridge is only sound when numbduck's loaded libduckdb is the same build the wheel uses.

findings.title: isinstance guard is not an ABI-layout proof: a spoofed/subclassed object turns the two chained from_address reads into attacker-influenced pointer dereferences
findings.category: type-confusion / arbitrary memory read via pointer arithmetic
findings.description: The only gate before the raw pointer walk is isinstance(conn, duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection) (line 52). isinstance is not a proof of memory layout: it is satisfied by (a) a subclass of DuckDBPyConnection, (b) any object whose metaclass overrides __instancecheck__, or (c) an object with a spoofed __class__, none of which guarantee the pybind11 simple-holder header at +16 or the unique_ptr<Connection> at +32. For any such object, id(conn)+16 reads a word from within/after that object's header and treats it as a C++ object pointer (cpp_obj_p, line 59); cpp_obj_p+32 then dereferences THAT value as an address (line 62) — an attacker-influenced, essentially arbitrary pointer read. The resulting conn_ptr is then passed to duckdb_query (line 67). So a caller that passes a crafted object that merely answers True to isinstance drives two chained wild-pointer dereferences plus a C-API call on a bogus Connection*. bridge.md 3.1 notes the same: the guard 'guards the Python type only; it does not guarantee the pybind11/ABI layout matches'. This is a hardening gap rather than a boundary bypass (numbduck is a library, and a caller that wants to crash the process can do so directly), which is why it is low severity — but the isinstance check materially overstates the safety it provides, and the second read (line 62) in particular dereferences a value read out of the object, so it is a genuine attacker-influenced pointer deref, not merely a wrong-but-bounded offset.
findings.impact: A caller passing an isinstance-satisfying but layout-mismatched object (subclass, __instancecheck__/__class__ spoof) causes two chained arbitrary pointer dereferences and a duckdb_query on a garbage pointer -> segfault / undefined behavior, with no error path that can distinguish this from a legitimate connection until it crashes.
findings.recommendation: Treat the isinstance check as a convenience type-hint, not a safety guarantee, and document it as such. Where feasible tighten to an exact-type check (type(conn) is duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection) to reject subclasses, and pair the walk with the version/coordination guard (PBR-SEC-1) so the offsets are only trusted for the exact known-good build. Note in the docstring that a non-canonical DuckDBPyConnection is undefined behavior.

findings.title: Borrowed / use-after-free ownership contract of the returned pointer is undocumented (sibling documents it explicitly)
findings.description: extract_connection_ptr returns a bare int (line 74) that is a pointer BORROWED from conn: it stays valid only while conn is alive and open, and it cannot keep conn referenced. The docstring (lines 41-51) documents only the int return and the TypeError/RuntimeError, and says nothing about lifetime. A caller that stashes the returned int and uses it inside @njit after conn.close() or after conn is garbage-collected is dereferencing a freed/reset Connection* — a use-after-free. The sibling numbox bridge documents this contract prominently: pysqlite_bridge.extract_connection_ptr has a dedicated Returns note ('borrowed ... stays valid only while conn is alive and open') and a Warning section (pysqlite_bridge.py:132-144) spelling out that using the pointer after close()/GC is a use-after-free. numbduck's version drops that guidance entirely, so the most dangerous misuse of this API is silently undocumented. (This is the after-return UAF; the at-extraction null-after-close case is a separate correctness gap already noted for the COR unit.)
findings.impact: Callers unaware of the borrow semantics can build @njit code that dereferences a dangling duckdb_connection after close()/GC, a use-after-free that crashes or corrupts memory with no diagnostic. The omission is purely documentary but on a raw-pointer API the contract is the safety mechanism.
findings.recommendation: Add a Returns/Warning note mirroring numbox pysqlite_bridge: the returned int is a borrowed duckdb_connection owned by conn, valid only while conn is alive and open; the caller must retain conn for the full lifetime of any @njit use and must not use the pointer after conn.close() or GC.

notes: Scope is pybridge.py security only; COR-dimension items (missing version guard PBR-COR-1, null-after-close at extraction PBR-COR-2, overstated 'validated' wording PBR-COR-3) are already filed for PBR-COR and not duplicated here except where the security framing differs (SEC-3 covers the after-return UAF, distinct from COR-2's at-extraction null). The 48-byte create_duckdb_result buffer used by the validation query (line 65) is a real heap-OOB-write concern if duckdb_result grows within the <1.6 pin, but that allocator lives in duckdb_utils.py and is out of this unit's target. get_unicode_data_p("SELECT 1") (line 66) is not a lifetime bug: the literal is held in the function's co_consts. The strongest, most SEC-specific finding is PBR-SEC-1 (cross-library type confusion), which is concretely reachable via the macOS/standalone loader fallback and NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB/brew paths and is exactly the failure numbox's libraries_coordinated() gate exists to prevent; pybridge omits that gate.
